data.name: Currency Exchange Converter
data.description: Full-stack app thag allows users to monitor current currency exchange rates
data.imgAlt: Home page of the foreign currency exchange rate calculator. A ticker displaying the exchange rates for various currencies is at the top. In the middle are two input fields, one labeled "Send" and the other labeled "Receive." A line chart showing the current exchange rate over time is at the bottom.
data.functionality:
The app lets you check exchange rates for 55 different currencies. Users can enter an amount to send and see the conversion in real time as they type. They can select the "send" and "receive" currencies from a searchable currency picker. They can also swap the "send" and "receive" currencies with the "swap" button, favorite the active pair, and log a conversion to their history.
Additionally, they can view a ticker of currency pairs, each with its current rate and 24-hour change, as well as line and area charts of the active pair's rate over time.
Users can see a log of their conversions, each of which shows the time, pair, and send and receive amounts. Logs can be exported as a CSV file. Favorites and logs are stored in a database. Because of this, users can either create an account or continue as a guest. Guests can link their session to a Google account to become permanent users.
data.whatILearned:
This was the first major project that I built from scratch using Next.js App Router. I learned how to implement server-side and client-side routing, as well as how proxies work. In addition, I learned a couple of new Tailwind classes and how to use Supabase with server-side rendering.
For this project, I implemented an authentication flow that included OAuth 2.0 with Supabase. I learned how to properly implement server-side rendering. Additionally, I improved my SQL skills by writing triggers and functions for my database and applying row-level security to my tables.
data.continuedDevelopment: In the future, I would like to improve the accessibility of my projects. This project includes line charts, an area that I feel is lacking. I also want to write tests for my components and tidy up the project structure.

data.name: Savings Tracker
data.description: Full-stack app that helps users manage their finances more easily
data.imgAlt: Savings Tracker Dashboard: At the top, you'll see the logo and a button labeled "New Goal." In the middle is an overview of statistics such as total savings, active goals, and completed goals. The goals section is at the bottom.
data.functionality:
The app lets you set savings goals with a target amount and an optional deadline. Goals can be filtered and sorted alphabetically, by highest or lowest progress, or by deadline to make it easier to keep track.
After creating a goal, you can make deposits toward it and view your deposit history. Also, bar charts compare your savings for each month.
Goals and deposits are stored in a database. This is why users can create an account to save their data. However, they can also continue as a guest. They can log in with an email address and password or with their Google account.
data.whatILearned: This was the second project I built with Next.js. I learned how the App Router works, as well as how to customize a proxy. I also practiced using linear gradients and background images with Tailwind CSS. I also created custom trigger functions for the Supabase backend and practiced implementing OAuth in my applications. I also learned a lot about accessibility. For example, I learned how to create a dashboard that can be fully navigated with the keyboard.
data.continuedDevelopment: In the future, I want to improve the accessibility of my projects. Also, there is a bug that occurs when reloading the goal details page. The not-found page is shown even though the goal exists. I want to fix that.

data.name: Tic Tac Toe Game
data.description: Classic game that you can play alone or with friends
data.imgAlt: This is the game screen for Tic-Tac-Toe. A box at the top indicates whose turn it is. The nine game squares are in the middle. Some squares are filled with an X or an O. The statistics are displayed at the bottom: X wins, O wins, and ties.
data.functionality:
For this one, I recreated the well-known game tic-tac-toe as a web application. Players can choose to play against an intelligent computer opponent or each other.
Players can choose to play as X or O, but remember that X goes first. Opponents then take turns until someone has a combo of three fields in a row or along the diagonal axis, or until all fields are filled.
The app provides statistics for each session and saves the current game state in local storage. This allows you to easily return to a previous session. The computer opponent calculates the best available moves. Do you think you have what it takes to beat it?
data.whatILearned: During this project, I sharpened my problem-solving skills by programming an intelligent CPU opponent that makes it difficult to win. I also practiced my React and Tailwind skills. In addition, I used React Router to navigate between the start and game screens.
data.continuedDevelopment: In the future, I would like to improve the accessibility of my project, as this is the area in which it is lacking the most.

data.name: Hangman Game
data.description: Guess the word - 8 incorrect guesses and you're out
data.imgAlt: Game screen for the Hangman game. The category is displayed at the top. In this case, the category is "Capitals." In the middle are boxes that are either filled in for guessed letters or left empty for unguessed letters. A keyboard is displayed at the bottom, with some letters grayed out.
data.functionality:
We've all played Hangman before. You can choose from six different categories, including TV shows and capital cities. Then, you are presented with a word or multiple words that you must guess correctly.
Players may guess as many times as they like. However, after eight incorrect guesses, they are eliminated. When a correct letter is guessed, all occurrences of that letter in the target word are revealed. If a guess is incorrect, the respective letter button turns gray and becomes disabled.
During the game, you can quit or switch categories. Once the game is over, you can restart it with the same category. There are plenty of words to guess, so don't worry about the game becoming repetitive.
data.whatILearned: This was one of the first projects I built with React. I learned a lot about state management and when to use useState. I also learned a lot about effects in React. Lastly, I improved my accessibility skills after completing this challenge.
data.continuedDevelopment: In the future, I would like to work on achieving a perfect accessibility score for this project and refining the design.
